title: Moving People in Real Time
description: Design a ride-sharing system with geohashing, driver matching, real-time GPS tracking, ETA estimation, and dynamic surge pricing.

segments.text: You tap a button, and within seconds a driver is matched, a route is calculated, and an ETA appears. Uber processes millions of rides daily across thousands of cities. Let's design the system behind that magic.
The core challenge: finding nearby drivers. You can't scan every driver on the planet. You need spatial indexing — a way to quickly find all drivers within a few kilometers of the rider's location.

Geohashing converts a two-dimensional latitude and longitude into a one-dimensional string. Nearby locations share common prefixes. 'dr5ru' and 'dr5rv' are neighboring cells. Finding nearby drivers becomes a simple prefix query.

Every active driver sends GPS updates every few seconds. The location service updates the driver's geohash in a fast store like Redis. When a rider requests a ride, the system queries the rider's geohash cell and its eight neighbors.
You've found ten available drivers near the rider. Three are one kilometer away, but two of those are heading in the opposite direction. Which driver should you match?
segments.thought_prompt: What factors besides raw distance should the matching algorithm consider?

segments.text: The matching algorithm considers ETA — not just distance but actual driving time. A driver five hundred meters away but stuck behind a one-way street might take longer than a driver one kilometer away on a clear road heading your direction.

ETA calculation uses historical road speed data segmented by time of day, day of week, and real-time traffic signals. Machine learning models predict travel time more accurately than simple distance-over-speed calculations.

Once matched, the driver's location streams to the rider in real time. The driver's GPS updates flow through a WebSocket connection. The rider's app renders the car moving on the map, updated every second or two.
It's New Year's Eve. Ride requests spike ten times above normal. There aren't enough drivers to serve everyone. Riders wait twenty minutes. Drivers earn normal rates.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you balance supply and demand when ride requests far exceed available drivers?

segments.text: Surge pricing. When demand exceeds supply in a geohash region, prices increase dynamically. Higher prices reduce demand from price-sensitive riders and incentivize more drivers to enter the area. The multiplier adjusts in real time as the balance shifts.

The dispatch system orchestrates everything: ride request intake, driver matching, trip state machine — requested, matched, en route, in progress, completed. Each state transition triggers events for tracking, billing, and analytics.

Ride-sharing is spatial computing at scale. Geohashing for proximity queries, ETA models for smart matching, WebSockets for real-time tracking, and dynamic pricing for supply-demand equilibrium. Every component must work in real time, every second counts.
